evidence: FulfilmentService constructor injects the ProductRepository and OrderRepository interfaces, so there is no persistence implementation in the file
advanceOrder and cancelOrder hand state changes to order.advanceTo(), order.cancel() and product.release()
placeOrder checks stock on all lines before any product.reserve() call, keeping a multi-product request atomic
toProductView and toOrderView turn domain objects into view objects for callers
combineItems validates the request (at least one item, a product id on every item, positive whole-number quantities). These checks arguably belong in Order: borderline, not counted as a violation
parsedVerdict.reasoning: FulfilmentService is an application service. Its responsibilities fit the application layer: it orchestrates use cases (addProduct, placeOrder, advanceOrder, cancelOrder, listOrders, getOrder), and it loads and saves through the injected ProductRepository and OrderRepository interfaces. It hands state changes to the domain objects (Order.advanceTo, Order.cancel, Product.reserve, Product.release), builds view objects (toProductView, toOrderView) and generates ids with randomUUID. It contains no transport code (HTTP or request/response handling) and no persistence, storage or framework code. The stock check in placeOrder runs across several products before any reservation, to keep a failed request atomic. That rule spans several aggregates, so it is legitimate application orchestration. combineItems merges duplicate request items and validates the input (at least one item, a product id on every item, positive whole-number quantities). These checks could arguably live in Order as domain rules. But the domain may already enforce them, and this is the borderline case of input validation inside an application service. The rubric's failure examples are a different layer kind entirely, such as infrastructure in the domain or business rules in infrastructure or presentation. So this is noted as a minor smell, not a clear violation.
